drills.name: The 'Backside Wall' Drill
drills.instructions: Set up with your tailbone just *barely* touching a wall or your golf bag. As you make your backswing, feel your *trail* (back) hip/glute push *back* into the wall, maintaining contact.

early_extension.human_explanation: This metric checks if your hips are thrusting *toward* the ball on your downswing. Your score was low because your hips moved forward, causing you to 'stand up' out of your posture. This is a very common flaw called 'Early Extension'.
early_extension.why_it_matters: This is a 'root cause' for topping or thinning your short irons. When your hips thrust forward, your whole body stands up, which *raises the bottom of your swing arc*. This causes you to hit the 'top' of the ball. It also blocks your arms, leading to pulls and poor contact.

drills.name: The 'Golf Bag' Drill
drills.instructions: Set up with your tailbone just *barely* touching your golf bag. Your goal is to make a full swing where your hips *rotate*, but do not 'push' the bag over. You should feel your trail hip stay back.

drills.name: The 'Chair' Drill
drills.instructions: Place a chair just behind your trail hip. As you start your downswing, feel like you are trying to 'sit back' into the chair. This is the 'pro' move of creating space by keeping your posture.

takeaway_path.human_explanation: This measures the path of your club in the first few feet of your swing. Your score was low because you 'pulled' the club 'inside' (behind your body). The 'pro' move is a 'one-piece' takeaway.
takeaway_path.why_it_matters: A major 'root cause' flaw. Pulling the club 'inside' right away gets it 'stuck' behind your body. This forces you to throw the club 'over-the-top' on the downswing to get back to the ball. This is a primary source of a slice.

drills.name: The 'Barrier' Drill
drills.instructions: Stick an alignment rod in the ground just *inside* your clubhead at address, angled to match your shaft. Your goal is to make your takeaway *without* hitting the rod. This forces you to keep the club 'on plane' and 'outside' your hands.

drills.name: The 'Towel' Drill
drills.instructions: Tuck a small towel under your *lead* (front) armpit. Make 50% backswings. Your goal is to keep the towel 'pinned' by your arm for the entire takeaway. If you pull the club 'inside', your arm will separate from your body and you'll drop the towel.

shaft_shallowing_downswing.human_explanation: This is a key pro-level metric. It measures if you 'shallow' the club (flatten it) on the downswing. Your score was low because you 'steepened' the club, which is a primary cause of an 'over-the-top' path.
shaft_shallowing_downswing.why_it_matters: Shallowing the club is the secret to attacking 'from the inside.' Steepening the club forces you to chop down on the ball, leading to pulls, slices, or thin contact.

drills.name: The 'Trail Elbow Down' Drill
drills.instructions: As you start your downswing, focus on driving your trail (back) elbow *down* towards your trail hip. This will naturally 'drop' the club into a shallower, more powerful slot behind you.

drills.name: The 'Drop and Turn' Drill
drills.instructions: From the top of your swing, feel like you pause and make a slight lateral shift with your lower body *before* your arms move. This forces the club to 'fall' onto a shallower plane before you rotate through.

backswing_width.human_explanation: This measures how 'wide' your swing arc is. Your score was low because your arms are 'collapsing' (getting too close to your head) at the top. Pros create power by maintaining a wide arc.
backswing_width.why_it_matters: Width is speed and consistency. A 'narrow' swing with 'collapsed' arms has a small arc and no speed. It's a major 'root cause' that forces you to 'cast' the club from the top, leading to an 'over-the-top' path.

drills.name: The 'Straight Arm' Takeaway
drills.instructions: For the first part of your backswing, feel like your *lead* (front) arm stays perfectly straight and 'pushes' the club away. This sets the width for the entire swing.

drills.name: The 'Ball Squeeze' Drill
drills.instructions: Place a small, partially-deflated beach ball or pillow between your forearms. Make 50% swings. Your goal is to keep the ball *squeezed* between your arms all the way to the top. If your arms 'collapse', you'll drop the ball.

wrist_release_impact.human_explanation: This measures the stability of your lead wrist *at* impact. Your score was low because your wrist 'flipped' or 'bent back' through the ball. Pros maintain a solid, firm wrist through the hitting area.
wrist_release_impact.why_it_matters: Flipping the wrist is a disaster for short irons. It moves the low point *behind* the ball (causing fat shots), adds loft (killing distance), and makes the ball curve uncontrollably. You must maintain a firm wrist through impact.

drills.name: The 'L-to-L' Drill
drills.instructions: Make a short swing (half-speed). Create a perfect 'L' shape in your lead arm and club in your backswing, and your goal is to finish the follow-through with the exact same 'L' shape. This stops the flipping motion.

drills.name: The 'Lead Arm Only' Impact Drill
drills.instructions: Place your trail hand on your side and hit small 30% shots using only your lead arm. It is physically impossible to 'flip' the wrist this way; it forces you to hit through the ball with a solid lead wrist.

spine_tilt_address.human_explanation: This measures your spine tilt *away* from the target at setup. Your score was low because your spine was too level or tilting forward. Wedges demand a very neutral, centered setup to promote a descending strike.
spine_tilt_address.why_it_matters: A neutral spine tilt is the key to achieving the steep `angle_of_attack` needed for spin. Tilting too far back encourages a scoop, leading to thin and topped shots.

drills.name: The 'Tee Under Lead Arm' Drill
drills.instructions: Place a tee under your lead (front) armpit. Make swings trying to keep the tee in place. This forces your lead shoulder to stay high, naturally creating the slight tilt away from the target.

drills.name: The 'Hip Bump' Drill
drills.instructions: Set up normally. Now, 'bump' your lead hip 1 inch toward the target. You will feel your spine automatically tilt back slightly. This is the perfect setup key for a wedge.

hip_sway_backswing.human_explanation: This measures how much your hips move 'side-to-side' in your backswing. Your score was low because your hips 'swayed' *away* from the target. Wedges demand a purely rotational swing around a fixed center.
hip_sway_backswing.why_it_matters: A 'hip sway' is the #1 root cause for inconsistent contact with wedges. It shifts your swing center, forcing you to 'hang back' on your downswing. This causes you to hit fat or thin shots.

drills.name: The 'Wall' Drill (or Golf Bag)
drills.instructions: Set up with your *trail* (back) hip just touching a wall or your golf bag. Your goal is to make a full backswing and feel your hip *rotate*, but *without* 'pushing' hard into the wall.

drills.name: The 'One-Leg' Drill
drills.instructions: Set up, then lift your *lead* (front) foot just off the ground. Now, try to make a slow, half-backswing. If you 'sway', you will lose your balance immediately. This forces you to 'rotate' around your trail leg.

hip_sway_impact.human_explanation: This measures your 'weight shift.' Your score was low because your hips 'hung back.' Pros shift their hips *aggressively forward* (4-6 inches) to lead the downswing and guarantee ball-first contact.
hip_sway_impact.why_it_matters: With wedges, this is essential. Shifting your hips forward moves the bottom of your swing *in front* of the ball, guaranteeing a crisp, 'ball-first' strike and maximum compression. 'Hanging back' is the #1 cause of poor wedge strikes.

drills.name: The 'Step-Through' Drill
drills.instructions: Hit an easy 70% shot. As you swing *through* impact, let your *back* foot come off the ground and take a full step *forward*. It's impossible to do this if your weight is stuck on your back foot.

drills.name: The 'Bump the Bag' Drill
drills.instructions: Place your golf bag on the *outside* of your *lead* foot. Your very first move in the downswing should be to 'bump' the bag with your lead hip. This teaches you the 'lateral shift' before rotation.

head_position_impact.human_explanation: This measures your head's position at impact. Your score was low because your head 'lunged' *forward*. Pros keep their head *stable* and slightly *behind* the ball to maintain the axis.
head_position_impact.why_it_matters: When your head lunges forward, you shift the low point of your swing forward too quickly, causing 'thin' contact. Maintaining a stable head is critical for a clean strike with a descending angle.

drills.name: The 'Back Foot Ball' Drill
drills.instructions: Place another ball (or headcover) on the ground *inside* your *trail* (back) foot. As you swing, your *only* focus is to keep your head 'over' that second ball. This feel will stop you from lunging forward.

drills.name: The 'Alignment Stick' Drill
drills.instructions: Have a friend hold an alignment stick or club vertically, just touching the *lead* (front) side of your head at address. Your goal is to make a full swing *without* hitting the stick.

lag_loss_downswing.human_explanation: This measures 'lag,' the 'snap' in your swing. Your score was low because you are 'casting' or 'throwing' the club from the top. Pros 'store' this angle and release it only at the ball.
lag_loss_downswing.why_it_matters: Casting is the #1 cause of inconsistent wedge strikes. It moves the low point of your swing *behind* the ball, leading to fat, thin, and weak shots.

drills.name: The 'Pump' Drill
drills.instructions: Make your backswing. On the way down, 'pump' the club twice: swing down to where your hands are at your hip (feeling the 'lag' angle), go back to the top, then 'pump' again. On the third 'pump', swing all the way through.

drills.name: The 'Trail Hand Off' Drill
drills.instructions: Hit 50% shots with *only* your lead hand on the club. It is *impossible* to 'cast' the club this way. This will force you to use your *body* to pull the club through and will build the 'lag' feeling.

arm_extension_finish.human_explanation: This measures how 'wide' you finish. Your score was low because your lead arm was 'bent' (a 'chicken wing'). Pros finish 'high and wide' with both arms extended.
arm_extension_finish.why_it_matters: A 'chicken wing' finish is a *symptom* of a flaw that happened *before* impact. It's almost always caused by an 'over-the-top' path or 'hip thrust' (Early Extension), which forces you to pull your arms in to avoid a disastrous strike.

drills.name: The 'Throw the Club' Drill
drills.instructions: Hit a 50% shot. After impact, your *only* thought is to feel like you are 'throwing' the clubhead as far *down the target line* as possible. This forces your arms to extend.

drills.name: The 'One-Arm Only' Drill
drills.instructions: Hit very small, 30% speed shots using *only* your lead arm. This forces you to use your *body* to pull the club through, which builds the correct extended release.

lead_leg_stabilization_impact.human_explanation: This measures the flex in your lead (front) knee at impact. Your score was low because your lead knee was too 'bent.' Pros straighten their lead leg to create a stable, rotational 'post'.
lead_leg_stabilization_impact.why_it_matters: The lead leg is the anchor for iron power. Straightening it provides a solid 'post' to rotate around, which is essential for transferring power and preventing your hips from swaying forward. A bent lead knee absorbs power.

drills.name: The 'Hips to the Wall' Drill
drills.instructions: Get into your impact position (hips forward). Now, try to rotate your hips so your back pockets point at the target. This feel *requires* you to post up and lock out your lead leg.

drills.name: The 'Foot Flare' Drill
drills.instructions: Flare (point out) your lead foot 30 degrees at address. This makes it easier for the lead leg to rotate and straighten, encouraging you to 'post up' and use the leg as a brace.

finish_balance_hold.human_explanation: This measures how stable your final pose is. Your score was low because you finished off-balance (falling back or taking a step). A good swing always ends in a rock-solid pose.
finish_balance_hold.why_it_matters: Poor balance at the finish confirms that your swing sequence was incorrect. Falling *backward* means your weight was stuck on your trail foot (no power). Falling *forward* means your upper body lunged too early. Fixing your balance means fixing your timing.

drills.name: The 'Foot Together' Finish
drills.instructions: After you hit the ball, your goal is to bring your trail (back) foot next to your lead foot and hold your perfect finish pose for a count of three. If you can't, your balance was off.

drills.name: The 'Trail Heel Up' Drill
drills.instructions: After impact, your focus is to get your trail heel as high off the ground as possible while maintaining balance. This forces 100% of your weight onto your lead leg.

head_movement_lateral.human_explanation: This measures how much your head moves 'side-to-side' in your backswing. Your score was low because your head 'swayed' *away* from the target. Wedges demand a fixed center.
head_movement_lateral.why_it_matters: A 'swaying' head is a classic *symptom* of a 'hip sway.' When your head moves off the ball, your entire swing center shifts, causing fat/thin contact. Fixing your hips fixes your head.

drills.name: The 'Nose on the Wall' Drill
drills.instructions: Set up in your posture at home with your nose *just* touching a wall. Make slow backswings. You will instantly feel if your head 'sways'.

drills.name: The 'Root Cause' Fix
drills.instructions: Your head sway is caused by your 'hip sway.' Your #1 fix is to practice the 'Wall Drill' for your hips. When you learn to *rotate*, your head will automatically stay centered.

shoulder_turn_top.human_explanation: This measures the 'tilt' of your shoulder turn. Your score was low because your shoulders are 'spinning' too 'flat'. Wedges require a very steep 'tilted' turn for control.
shoulder_turn_top.why_it_matters: Wedges demand a steep path. A 'flat' shoulder turn is a major power leak and root cause for the club getting stuck or swinging 'over-the-top.' A proper 'tilted' turn keeps the club on the correct, steep plane.

drills.name: The 'Club Across Shoulders' Drill
drills.instructions: Place a club across your shoulders and get into your address posture. Tilt your shoulders so the butt-end of the club points *down* at the ground.

drills.name: The 'Lead Shoulder Down' Feel
drills.instructions: As you make your backswing, your *only* thought should be 'lead shoulder to the back foot's big toe.' This feel forces your lead shoulder to work *down* and *across*.

shaft_lean_address.human_explanation: This measures your shaft lean at setup. Your score was low because your hands were 'neutral' or behind the ball. For wedges, pros set up with their hands *in front* of the ball.
shaft_lean_address.why_it_matters: Forward shaft lean is *mandatory* for compressing the ball with a wedge. This setup pre-sets the descending angle needed for spin and guarantees a ball-first strike.

drills.name: The 'Lead Hip Forward' Drill
drills.instructions: Set up normally. Now, lean the shaft forward until the butt-end of the club points at your *lead* hip. This forces the correct forward lean.

drills.name: The 'Handle Forward' Drill
drills.instructions: Hit 50% shots while keeping your lead arm and the shaft in one straight line through impact. This is the feel of maintaining the forward lean.

spine_tilt_impact.human_explanation: This measures your spine tilt *away* from the target at impact. Your score was low because your upper body 'lunged' forward, making your spine too vertical or tilting toward the target.
spine_tilt_impact.why_it_matters: Maintaining a near-vertical spine tilt at impact is crucial for precision. Losing this stability causes an inconsistent low point and thin contact.

drills.name: The 'Head Back' Drill
drills.instructions: Your spine tilt is a *result* of your head position. Your #1 fix is to practice the 'Back Foot Ball' drill. Focus *only* on keeping your head behind the ball through impact. Your spine will naturally stay tilted.

angle_of_attack.human_explanation: This is the key to hitting your wedges. Your score was low because your angle was too shallow (not steep enough). The goal with a wedge is to hit down *aggressively* to maximize spin and control.
angle_of_attack.why_it_matters: The shorter the club, the steeper the attack. Hitting down compresses the ball against the ground, creating massive backspin for control. Scooping is the #1 cause of weak, inconsistent wedge shots.

drills.name: The 'Line' Drill
drills.instructions: Draw a line on the ground. Your goal is to take a divot that *starts* on the 'target side' of the line. This forces you to hit down with authority.

drills.name: The 'Towel' Drill (Aggressive)
drills.instructions: Place a small, folded towel on the ground about 6 inches *behind* your ball. Your goal is to hit the ball *without* touching the towel. This eliminates 'scooping' and 'hanging back'.

club_path.human_explanation: This measures the direction your club is swinging at impact. A neutral path (0.0°) or slightly 'in-to-out' path (+0.5°) is ideal for controlling trajectory and spin.
club_path.why_it_matters: Wedges demand control. While we encourage a slight draw path for power, an 'out-to-in' slice path is a massive error that cuts across the ball, severely killing spin and control. We want a neutral, straight path.

drills.name: The 'Gate' Drill (Fix for a Slice)
drills.instructions: Place two headcovers on the ground to form a 'gate' for your club to swing through. This forces you to swing from the inside and neutralizes your 'out-to-in' slice path.

drills.name: The 'Hands In' Feel (Fix for a Hook)
drills.instructions: This is a feel drill for players who swing *too* 'in-to-out'. As you swing through impact, feel like your hands are staying 'closer' to your body. This will neutralize the hook.

spine_bend_address.human_explanation: This measures your forward bend from your hips. Your score was low because you are not bent over enough. With a short club like a wedge, you must hinge the most from your hips to get steeper and maintain balance.
spine_bend_address.why_it_matters: A lack of forward bend prevents you from hitting down on the ball, which is essential for wedge play. A proper, deep hip hinge ensures your body is set up to deliver the steep, descending strike needed for spin and control.

drills.name: The 'Hip Hinge' Drill
drills.instructions: Stand straight, club across your shoulders. Now, push your hips *straight back* (like closing a car door with your butt) until you feel a stretch in your hamstrings. That's the hinge you need for your short game.

drills.name: The 'Club on Back' Drill
drills.instructions: Hold a club vertically along your spine, making sure it touches your tailbone AND the back of your head. Now, perform the 'Hip Hinge' drill. If the club stays in contact with both points, your back is straight. If it loses contact, you are 'slumping'.

shoulder_plane_top.human_explanation: This measures the 'tilt' of your shoulder turn. Your score was low because your shoulders are 'spinning' too 'flat' (level with the ground). Pros turn on a very steep 'tilt,' with their lead shoulder working deep down and under.
shoulder_plane_top.why_it_matters: Wedges demand a steep, controlled path. A 'flat' shoulder turn is a major power leak and root cause for the club getting stuck or swinging 'over-the-top.' A proper 'tilted' turn keeps the club on the correct, steep plane.

drills.name: The 'Club Across Shoulders' Drill
drills.instructions: Place a club across your shoulders and get into your address posture. Now, make your backswing turn. Your goal is to tilt your shoulders so the butt-end of the club points *down* at the ground, well inside your ball's target line. If it points 'out' (level to the ground), your turn is too flat.

drills.name: The 'Lead Shoulder Down' Feel
drills.instructions: This is a feel drill. As you make your backswing, your *only* thought should be 'lead shoulder to the back foot's big toe.' This feel forces your lead shoulder to work *down* and *across*, creating the necessary steep, pro-level tilt.

trail_leg_flex_top.human_explanation: This measures the flex in your trail (back) leg at the top. Your score was low because your leg is 'locking' (straightening) too much. Pros maintain their flex, using their trail leg as a 'stable post' to rotate against.
trail_leg_flex_top.why_it_matters: When your trail leg 'locks' straight, it's impossible for your hips to turn correctly. This is a major 'root cause' that *forces* your hips to 'sway' off the ball, which leads to fat/thin contact and a loss of power.

drills.name: The 'Pressure on Instep' Drill
drills.instructions: This is a feel drill. As you make your backswing, your *only* thought should be to keep pressure on the *instep* (the inside) of your trail foot. If you 'lock' your leg, you will feel the pressure roll to the *outside* of your foot.

drills.name: The 'One-Knee' Drill
drills.instructions: Take your address. Now, slightly 'kick in' your trail knee (toward your lead knee). Your goal is to make a backswing and *keep* that inward-pointing knee flex. This will feel like a powerful 'brace' and stop you from locking your leg.

wrist_set_top.human_explanation: This measures your lead wrist position at the top. Your score was low because your wrist is 'cupped' (bent backwards). For wedges, a 'flat' or 'bowed' wrist is vital for face control and spin.
wrist_set_top.why_it_matters: A 'cupped' wrist is a primary cause of an open clubface, which kills spin and makes trajectory unpredictable. A 'flat' or 'bowed' wrist squares the face early, allowing you to attack aggressively without worrying about slicing.

drills.name: The 'Motorcycle' Drill
drills.instructions: As you get to the top of your swing, feel like you are revving a motorcycle with your lead hand. This 'bowing' motion will flatten your wrist and square the clubface. Hit 50% shots just feeling this move.

drills.name: The 'Hanger' Drill
drills.instructions: Get a plastic clothes hanger and clip it to your grip. Make a backswing. If your wrist is 'cupped', the hook of the hanger will *come off* your lead forearm. If you are 'flat', it will *stay pressed against* your forearm.

takeaway_path.human_explanation: This measures the path of your club in the first few feet of your swing. Your score was low because you 'pulled' the club 'inside' (behind your body). The wedge demands a very straight-back, controlled takeaway.
takeaway_path.why_it_matters: Pulling the club 'inside' on the takeaway gets the club 'stuck' behind your body. This forces you to throw the club 'over-the-top' on the downswing, which is a slice path that kills wedge spin and control.

drills.name: The 'Two-Tee Gate' Drill
drills.instructions: Place one tee just outside the toe of your club and one tee just inside the heel, about 1 foot back. Your goal is to swing the club *perfectly* between the two tees. This teaches a straight-back takeaway.

drills.name: The 'Towel' Drill
drills.instructions: Tuck a small towel under your *lead* (front) armpit. Make half-swings. Your goal is to keep the towel 'pinned' by your arm for the entire takeaway. If you pull the club 'inside', your arm will separate from your body and you'll drop the towel.

swing_tempo_ratio.human_explanation: This measures the rhythm of your swing. Your score was low because you are rushing your transition. The ideal professional tempo is 3-to-1: three times longer on the backswing than the downswing.
swing_tempo_ratio.why_it_matters: Tempo is the key to consistency. Rushing the transition destroys the sequence, causing the upper body to take over, which is the root cause for 'casting' and swinging 'over-the-top.' Slowing down the backswing allows the lower body time to start the downswing.

drills.name: The '1-2-3, HIT!' Drill
drills.instructions: Make your backswing while counting 'One, two, three.' Start your downswing on 'Hit!' This forces a 3:1 rhythm and builds patience at the top of the swing.

drills.name: The 'Pause' Drill
drills.instructions: At the top of your swing, consciously pause for one full second before starting the downswing. This ensures you complete your backswing coil and allows the lower body to initiate the change of direction.
